name: Kernel

modes.label: Headless
modes.note: One GB active browser runtime; idle standby free.

modes.label: Headful (8 or 16 GiB)
modes.note: Headful Chromium with Live View + computer controls API; $0.0000166667/GB-second: 8 GiB default ($0.48/h), 16 GiB when `memory` is set on create ($0.96/h). No guaranteed CPU count.

modes.label: Headful GPU
modes.note: Start-Up+ only; USD 0.0008000016/s (48x the GB-second rate); no standby (billed until deleted); us-east only; not available in browser pools. GPU model unpublished.

modes.label: App invocation (serverless agent code, 4 GB)
modes.note: USD 0.0000666668/s = USD 0.24/h at 4 GB; billed only while code runs; browsers billed separately; invocation concurrency 5/10/50 (20 per app on Start-Up).

plans.name: Start-Up
plans.note: GPU, regional browsers and BYO proxy; 30-day replays. App concurrency 50 org / 20 per app. Free trial offered (length not published); priority email support; browser pools, unlimited custom extensions/projects, audit log export.

plans.name: Enterprise
plans.note: SSO, HIPAA BAA, dedicated support, ZDR, custom limits.

features.ip_note: Direct egress by default; Kernel-provided datacenter, ISP, residential and mobile proxies are unmetered (fair use); stealth mode adds a static ISP proxy + CAPTCHA solver; BYO proxy on Start-Up/Enterprise.

caveats: Storage, snapshot GiB-month and public IPv4 prices are not published in the reviewed sources; null is not free.

No guaranteed vCPU allocation published; browser-hour is not a verified 4-vCPU/8-GiB VM equivalent. The sizes card keeps unknown hardware null; do not coerce it to zero or auto-rank against resource-guaranteed VMs.
Browser RAM is not published unless a specific mode overrides it.
The homepage GB-second rate and docs preset rates agree: 1 GB headless, 8 GB headful. 16 GB is a documented headful option. Do not charge CPU+RAM again on top.
Standby billing is based on browser activity, not CPU utilization. An open active live view/CDP workload may prevent savings. Pool and standby browsers continue consuming concurrency.
Pool availability conflicts internally: feature table says all tiers; FAQ says Start-Up and Enterprise. Fifty-browser example already needs Start-Up.
Idle pool disks are free, but snapshot_gib_month stays null because general snapshot storage is not priced. Browser profiles are not general disks.

Headful = Chromium on a virtual display with Live View and a computer-controls API, not a full desktop environment; SSH into the browser VM is available (kernel browsers ssh). Headless has no Live View.

eu-west / ap-southeast browsers need the Start-Up or Enterprise plan. On Free and Hobbyist Kernel is US-only (us-east), so an EU/Asia workload must pay the USD 200 Start-Up plan. Model this as region-specific mode copies with plans:["Start-Up","Enterprise"], or as a plan gate.
16 GiB headful price (USD 0.96/h) is derived from the GB-second definition; the docs pricing table lists only one headful rate (USD 0.0001333336/s = 8 GB).
YC startups get a discount ('here's our yc deal'). Terms are behind a link and not published on the pricing page.

knobs.label: Fraction outside standby
knobs.why: Standby begins after 5 seconds without CDP/live-view activity, not at low CPU use.

fleet.notes: Quota is org-wide and includes reserved browser-pool capacity and standby browsers, even idle/unacquired. 10 fits Hobbyist, 50 Start-Up, 300/1,000 Enterprise. App invocation concurrency is separate. Per-project concurrency caps (org default + per-project override) sit under the org cap. API requests are rate-limited per organization (HTTP 429 + Retry-After); the numeric limit is unpublished and raised via contact.

audit_2026_09_29.source: checked against the provider's live pricing and docs pages

snapshot_auto.quote: One of the most powerful features of our approach is the ability to create complete snapshots of the browser's state when entering standby mode. These snapshots capture everything:
snapshot_auto.note: Trigger: standby after 5 s with no CDP/WebDriver/Live View/computer-controls activity ('Kernel browsers automatically enter standby after `five seconds` with no activity', /docs/browsers/standby). Memory included: list includes 'Loaded page content and DOM state' and 'Active downloads and processes'; restored 'in milliseconds' on next connection. Limits: the standby browser is still deleted after its timeout (default 60 s, max 72 h) counted from standby, so the snapshot does not outlive the session; 'GPU-accelerated browsers do not support standby mode.'

snapshot_on_demand.note: No snapshot/checkpoint/fork endpoint in the full OpenAPI spec or docs. Closest: browser profiles (cookies/storage/browser state) that are saved when a browser with save_changes is deleted or times out ('When the Kernel browser is deleted or times out, Kernel replaces the stored profile with that browser's complete state.') and loaded by new browsers - browser state only, not a machine/memory snapshot. Browser pools keep pre-warmed browsers.

harness_api.note: No endpoints to start/stream/resume Claude Code, Codex or a Kernel agent inside the browser VM. Kernel apps (deploy/invoke/invocation events) run your own code; process exec/spawn is a generic exec API; Managed Auth is a narrow login agent; Claude Code integration is Kernel as an MCP server/skills used FROM Claude Code, not a harness inside Kernel.

ingress_rules.note: Browser VMs expose no arbitrary public ports; access is only via per-session tokenized CDP/WebDriver/Live View URLs (Live View can be read-only) and API-authenticated 'kernel browsers ssh' with -L/-R port forwarding. No IP allowlists or user-chosen public port URLs. Network-access page: 'You don't need to open inbound ports.'

secret_proxy.quote: fill isn't secret isolation from the browser. an agent with unrestricted browser access, page scripts, or extensions can read values after filling.
secret_proxy.note: Vault 'fill' writes credentials into browser form fields (values enter the VM, hidden only from your app/model context); Managed Auth logs in and stores cookies in a profile; app secrets are env vars. Exception, payments only: agentcard integration gives the agent non-secret card aliases and Kernel intercepts the recognized checkout request at egress ('the card number and cvc stay with agentcard. your agent receives non-secret aliases.') - a true out-of-VM substitution but limited to card checkout formats, not arbitrary HTTP credentials. No coverage of DB/SSH/git.

volume_attach.note: No volume/disk resources in the API; storage is the ephemeral browser VM filesystem (File I/O API upload/download) plus browser profiles and extensions.

volume_shared.quote: Each browser session loads its own profile snapshot. Profiles don't synchronize changes between running browsers
volume_shared.note: One profile can be attached to many browsers but as a per-browser copy, not a live shared filesystem; no shared volumes.

isolation.quote: a Kernel browser is a unikernel VM with no shared host kernel — root inside your session has no path to other customers or platform infrastructure
isolation.note: Kernel's own docs describe each browser as a dedicated Unikraft-based unikernel VM (sub-20ms cold starts) but never name the underlying hypervisor. Unikraft's microVM deployment target is Firecracker/KVM, the closest enum match to 'unikernel VM with no shared host kernel'; not independently confirmed on Kernel's own pages.

image_oci.quote: running Chromium browsers on lightweight unikernels. This architecture represents a significant departure from traditional solutions (warm pools / Kubernetes-orchestrated Docker containers)
image_oci.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Machines are fixed Chromium-on-unikernel browser VMs or a code-deploy runtime (kernel deploy from source, no Dockerfile/config); there is no way to boot a custom OCI/Docker image.

nested_virt.quote: unikernels are specialized, single-purpose systems that include only the necessary components to run a specific application
nested_virt.note: derived: a minimal single-purpose unikernel VM has no documented /dev/kvm passthrough or nested-virtualization support; not mentioned anywhere in the docs.

snapshot.quote: the ability to create complete snapshots of the browser's state when entering standby mode. These snapshots capture everything: ... Active downloads and processes
snapshot.note: Automatic memory snapshot on standby (idle), restored on next connection; not a user-invoked persistent snapshot API (see snapshot_on_demand=false in the card).

fork.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. No clone/fork endpoint exists; browser pools pre-warm fresh identical browsers, not clones of a specific running machine's state.

fork_running.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. No forking capability of any kind is documented.

memory_snapshot_fork.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Kernel's memory snapshots (standby) resume the same session in place; they are not used to spawn a new, separate machine.

wake_on_request.quote: Your app can spring to life almost instantly when needed, then return to standby when idle.
wake_on_request.note: A new CDP/WebDriver/Live View/computer-controls connection to a standby browser automatically wakes it from its memory snapshot; no explicit 'resume' API call is required.

persistent_disk.quote: it will be automatically deleted after a configurable timeout (default 60 seconds)
persistent_disk.note: The browser VM's writable filesystem is deleted with the browser; only cookies/local-storage/extensions persist across sessions via Browser Profiles, not arbitrary files on disk.

live_resize.quote: 8 GiB default ($0.48/h), 16 GiB when `memory` is set on create ($0.96/h)
live_resize.note: Memory tier is chosen at browser creation time; no documented API to change CPU/RAM of an already-running browser. 'Resize at any time' in the docs refers to browser-pool size (instance count), not per-machine resources.

agent_harnesses.quote: kernel create --template claude-agent-sdk ... When deploying to Kernel, the app automatically installs Claude Code on the remote infrastructure.
agent_harnesses.note: Claude Agent SDK / Claude Code is offered as a first-party app template and auto-installed on deploy.

own_agent_api.quote: Kernel Agent: User-directed browser automation. Kernel Agent visits pages on behalf of an end user's request; it is not an automatic crawler.
own_agent_api.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. 'Kernel Agent' is a Web Bot Auth traffic-identity label for customer-run automation, not a first-party API that runs Kernel's own browsing/research agent on your behalf.

lang_python.quote: The dependency manifest (`package.json` for JS/TS, `pyproject.toml` for Python) must be present in the root directory of your project.
lang_python.note: Kernel apps and the SDK support Python; `kernel.browsers.repl()` etc. are also callable from the Python SDK.

lang_node.quote: Execute JavaScript in a persistent Node.js runtime that lives alongside Chromium inside your browser's VM.
lang_node.note: Node.js/TypeScript is a first-class supported runtime for both the REPL and app deployment.

public_ipv4.quote: You don't need to open inbound ports.
public_ipv4.note: Browser VMs are not assigned a routable public IPv4; access is only via Kernel-hosted, per-session tokenized CDP/Live View URLs.

inbound_https.note: Reachability is only through Kernel's own api.onkernel.com proxy endpoints (Live View/CDP tokens) or `kernel browsers ssh` port-forwarding; there is no way to expose an arbitrary app port on the machine over its own public HTTPS URL.

egress_allowlist.quote: To lock a browser to an approved set of URLs, block everything with `URLBlocklist` and then allow back only the URLs you want with `URLAllowlist`.
egress_allowlist.note: Chrome-policy level allow/deny list on top-level navigation domains/paths; it does not block sub-resource or API calls a permitted page loads from other origins, so it is narrower than a network-level security-group egress rule.

egress_http_rules.quote: Entries match a whole domain (`chatgpt.com`) or a specific path ... it does not block resources or API calls a permitted page loads from other origins.
egress_http_rules.note: URLAllowlist/URLBlocklist operate at domain/path granularity for page navigation, not at HTTP method level; no method-scoped egress rule is documented.

guest_firewall.quote: a Kernel browser is a unikernel VM with no shared host kernel — root inside your session has no path to other customers or platform infrastructure
guest_firewall.note: derived: full VM with root=true inside a real Linux process environment; nftables/iptables are not explicitly documented but expected to work given root shell access.

static_egress_ip.quote: every connection in a session exits through the same static IP — making them ideal for login flows and session-based workflows.
static_egress_ip.note: Available via Kernel's ISP proxy (or BYO custom proxy on Start-Up/Enterprise), not as a default per-machine egress IP.

windows.quote: Headless / Headful Chromium browsers on Linux unikernels
windows.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Kernel only offers Linux-based Chromium browser VMs; the only 'windows' string in the docs refers to residential-proxy OS geo-targeting, not a Windows machine.

macos.quote: Headless / Headful Chromium browsers on Linux unikernels
macos.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. No macOS machine option; the only 'macOS' mentions are local CLI install instructions and residential-proxy OS targeting.

self_host.quote: Kernel's infrastructure runs browsers on Unikraft-based unikernels hosted by Kernel
self_host.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Kernel is a managed SaaS (with a BYOC option deploying into the customer's own cloud account); there is no self-hosted/open-source build of the platform itself to run entirely on your own infrastructure.

eu_data_residency.quote: Choose from `us-east`, `eu-west`, and `ap-southeast`. Region selection is available on Start-Up and Enterprise plans
eu_data_residency.note: eu-west region is offered for browsers (Start-Up/Enterprise plans; Free/Hobbyist are US-only).

docker_inside.quote: running Chromium browsers on lightweight unikernels. This architecture represents a significant departure from traditional solutions (warm pools / Kubernetes-orchestrated Docker containers)
docker_inside.note: not offered: outside the product's scope. Machines are minimal, single-purpose Unikraft-based unikernel VMs ('unikernels typically lack internal security boundaries... include only the necessary components to run a specific application'); no dockerd/container runtime, systemd, or general-purpose OS is documented inside the browser VM or the app-invocation runtime. Consistent with nested_virt=false already recorded on this card.

max_session_h.quote: If you don't manually delete a browser, it will be automatically deleted after a configurable `timeout` (default 60 seconds). The timeout begins once the browser enters standby... You can set a custom timeout of up to 72 hours when creating a browser
max_session_h.note: The only documented auto-stop is an idle/standby deletion timer (default 60 s, configurable up to 259200 s = 72 h), and that countdown only starts once the browser has been inactive for 5 s (no CDP/WebDriver/Live View/computer-controls activity). A continuously-driven session ('A browser stays alive as long as something is driving it') has no documented absolute lifetime cap, so effectively it runs until you stop it, like a VM. GPU browsers additionally don't support standby and are 'billed until deleted' with no published hour cap either.
